newsitem.title: USA: OUTLOOK 1997 - A steady course seen for US housing.
newsitem.headline: OUTLOOK 1997 - A steady course seen for US housing.

text.p: Potential first-time homebuyers can cheer in the new year because U.S. mortgage rates are likely to stick to their current levels, said market experts.
And steady long-term interest rates usually soothe home-buying jitters, they said.

"There is going to be less volatility in mortgage rates, which gives people more of a stable sense and time to look around," said Eileen Neely, manager of economic forecasting for the Federal National Mortgage Association (Fannie Mae).
However, U.S. homeowners looking to refinance their mortgages will probably not welcome the new year with open ARMs.
Most ARMs -- adjustable-rate mortgages -- will not be ripe for refinancing unless rates sink below first-quarter 1996 levels, Neely said.

"As far as (homeowners) looking to refinance, there are going to be some opportunities, but not a whole lot if they have already taken advantage of the low rates in the beginning of this year or even two years ago," she said.
Currently, average mortgage rates are hovering near the 7.5 percent mark for 30-year fixed-rate loans, and many economists predict very little change in either direction for upcoming year.

Frank Nothaft, deputy chief economist for the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp (Freddie Mac), said he expects overall economic activity to pick up modestly in the first quarter, which will put some upward pressure on long-term rates.
"Next year, as a whole, we have mortgage rates averaging just about 7.7 percent for 30-year fixed-rate credit," he said. "That's a very little change from the current average."

Nothaft's credit outlook falls in line with the latest Reuters interest-rate survey of 25 economists, who forecast, on average, that the 30-year Treasury bond yield would stay mostly within a range of 6.4 percent to 6.5 percent throughout 1997.
Similarly, the pundits predicted, on average, that the federal funds rate would hold firm at around 5.25 percent throughout the year.

"The economy looks like it will grow at about 2.0 percent next year," said Nothaft, who did not participate in the Reuters poll. "That is a good environment for maintaining monetary policy at its current level and keeping interest rates very affordable."
But if the economy plods along at a slower pace next year, the labor markets may weaken enough to push unemployment rates higher, and eventually dampen consumer confidence, economists said.
"Ultimately, when consumer confidence gets a kick so does housing," said Fannie Mae's Neely.
Kurt Karl, an economist at WEFA Group, agreed. He said softer housing starts next year will probably stem from slower employment growth and less demand growth from fewer people getting new jobs.

Karl is calling for total housing starts to hit a 1.43 million annual rate in 1997, slightly lower than his forecast of 1.47 million in 1996. Specifically, Karl projected in 1997 a 300,000 annual rate for multi-family units and a 1.13 million annual rate forsingle-family units.
"There are certain cities that are just really in dire need of multi-family units," he said, citing San Francisco and Denver as two examples.
"So we don't see much of a falloff in multi-family units ... All of the falloff is in single-family (units)," he said.
Gopal Ahluwalia, director of research for the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), said modest declines in housing starts will eventually chip away at new home sales, albeit moderately.
Ahluwalia said 1997 new home sales should come close to an annualized rate of 658,000, lower than his forecast of 749,000 this year.
Likewise, he pegged existing home sales to an annualized rate of 3.6 million in 1997, down from his forecast of about 4.0 million in 1996.
Regionally, California will continue to lead the West in terms of the volume of home sales and levels of new construction, experts said.

Nothaft of Freddie Mac predicted that California would "generally show more growth than the rest of the country" next year, although its lead over the rest of the country will be narrower than in the past.

Neely concurred that California's housing market is recovering. She noted that in recent years, other states in the Pacific Northwest and Mountain region have bolstered the West during California's slump.
After California's labor market turned sour in the wake of defense cutbacks and aerospace industry problems, she said, many people abandoned their California dreams for the Mountain states.
For 1997, the mountain states will continue to perform well, Neely said, but California's labor market will continue to improve and so will its housing market.
Overall, most states are expected to perform relatively on par with their performance this year.
The housing sector will maintain its course as it has for the past couple of years, said WEFA Group's Karl.
It will be neither a boom nor a bust market, he said. "It's as steady as she goes."
-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1562
